claim: 37 viral samples were collected longitudinally from four immunocompromised patients with long-term H3N2 influenza infections in the 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 seasons.
source: We deep-sequenced 37 viral samples collected longitudinally from four immunocompromised patients with long-term H3N2 influenza infections in the 2005–2006 and 2006–2007 seasons (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1 showing the timeline of infections.

claim: The patients developed influenza infections in the months after receiving hematopoietic cell transplantations when immune cell counts were still low.
source: These patients developed influenza infections in the months after receiving hematopoietic cell transplantations when immune cell counts were still low, and nasal wash samples were collected approximately every week.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the patient population.

claim: All patients were treated with the neuraminidase inhibitor oseltamivir for at least some duration of their infections.
source: All patients were treated with the neuraminidase inhibitor oseltamivir for at least some duration of their infections (Campbell et al., 2015) (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Campbell et al., 2015 and reference to figures showing treatment timelines.

claim: De novo mutations arise most commonly in the surface proteins hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) across the influenza genome.
source: Across the influenza genome, de novo mutations arise most commonly in the surface proteins hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) (Figure 2A), which undergo rapid global evolution (Bhatt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A showing the distribution of mutations across genes, with citation to Bhatt et al., 2011 for global evolution.

claim: HA and NA undergo rapid global evolution.
source: Across the influenza genome, de novo mutations arise most commonly in the surface proteins hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) (Figure 2A), which undergo rapid global evolution (Bhatt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Bhatt et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations T242I and R292K in NA are associated with oseltamivir resistance.
source: In NA in particular, we observe the emergence and persistence of mutations T242I and R292K, which are known to be associated with oseltamivir resistance (Baz et al., 2006; van der Vries et al., 2013), a phenomenon of strong clinical importance (Renaud et al., 2011) (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Baz et al., 2006 and van der Vries et al., 2013.

claim: Nine sites in the influenza genome showed parallel mutations that arose in two or more patients: five in HA, three in NA, and one in the NS segment.
source: We identified nine sites in the influenza genome where parallel mutations arose in two or more patients in our study: five in HA, three in NA, and one in the nonstructural (NS) segment (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 7; HA: p<0.001; NA: p<0.01; permutation test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2C and statistical testing via permutation test.

claim: The parallel emergence of mutations in HA across multiple patients is statistically significant (p<0.001).
source: We identified nine sites in the influenza genome where parallel mutations arose in two or more patients in our study: five in HA, three in NA, and one in the nonstructural (NS) segment (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 7; HA: p<0.001; NA: p<0.01; permutation test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with p-value from permutation test.

claim: The parallel emergence of mutations in NA across multiple patients is statistically significant (p<0.01).
source: We identified nine sites in the influenza genome where parallel mutations arose in two or more patients in our study: five in HA, three in NA, and one in the nonstructural (NS) segment (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 7; HA: p<0.001; NA: p<0.01; permutation test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with p-value from permutation test.

claim: The influenza genome consists of eight linear segments that freely re-assort with one another but do not recombine.
source: The influenza genome consists of eight linear segments that freely re-assort with one another but do not recombine (Boni et al., 2008), meaning that each segment evolves clonally.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Boni et al., 2008.

claim: Each influenza genome segment evolves clonally.
source: The influenza genome consists of eight linear segments that freely re-assort with one another but do not recombine (Boni et al., 2008), meaning that each segment evolves clonally.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a consequence of the lack of recombination.

claim: Clonal interference has been characterized extensively in experimental evolution.
source: This phenomenon, known as clonal interference, has been characterized extensively in experimental evolution (Hegreness et al., 2006; Kao and Sherlock, 2008; Lang et al., 2013; Neher, 2013) and affects influenza's global evolution (Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with multiple citations to experimental evolution studies.

claim: Clonal interference affects influenza's global evolution.
source: This phenomenon, known as clonal interference, has been characterized extensively in experimental evolution (Hegreness et al., 2006; Kao and Sherlock, 2008; Lang et al., 2013; Neher, 2013) and affects influenza's global evolution (Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012.

claim: In patient X, lineages carrying S193Y and N225D initially compete, but a double-mutant carrying both mutations eventually fixes.
source: In patient X, lineages carrying S193Y and N225D initially compete, but a double-mutant carrying both mutations eventually fixes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B displaying haplotype frequencies over time.

claim: The A138S and F193Y mutations arise multiple times in parallel in patient W on distinct genetic backgrounds.
source: The A138S and F193Y mutations also arise multiple times in parallel in patient W: once on the ancestral haplotype '0000' to form the single-mutant '1000' and '0100' lineages; once on these single-mutant lineages to form the double-mutant '1100'; and once on the double-mutant '0011' to form the triple-mutant '1011' and '0111' lineages (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C displaying haplotype evolution.

claim: Several weeks into patient W's infection, at least five distinct HA lineages are present at a frequency of at least 5%.
source: Several weeks into patient W's infection, we observe at least five distinct HA lineages at a frequency of at least 5%, and the lineages differ from each other by one to three nonsynonymous mutations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In HA, most sites that varied within hosts also varied in the global influenza population.
source: In HA, most sites that varied within hosts also varied in the global influenza population, compared to about a quarter of such sites in the other influenza genes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B comparing within-host and global variation.

claim: About a quarter of sites that varied within hosts in non-HA genes also varied in the global influenza population.
source: In HA, most sites that varied within hosts also varied in the global influenza population, compared to about a quarter of such sites in the other influenza genes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is significant parallelism in HA evolution between within-host and global scales (p<0.01).
source: We found significant parallelism in HA (p<0.01), but not in NA or in the rest of the genome (p>0.05) when we consider all sites of global variation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on permutation testing.

claim: There is no significant parallelism in NA evolution between within-host and global scales (p>0.05).
source: We found significant parallelism in HA (p<0.01), but not in NA or in the rest of the genome (p>0.05) when we consider all sites of global variation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on permutation testing.

claim: There is no significant parallelism in the rest of the influenza genome (excluding HA and NA) between within-host and global scales (p>0.05).
source: We found significant parallelism in HA (p<0.01), but not in NA or in the rest of the genome (p>0.05) when we consider all sites of global variation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on permutation testing.

claim: Four of the five sites of recurrent within-host mutation in HA are also sites of global influenza variation.
source: In particular, four of the five sites of recurrent within-host mutation in HA are also sites of global influenza variation (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutation L427F reaches a frequency of >75% in three patients but is rare or nonexistent in influenza globally.
source: However, the concordance is incomplete. Mutation L427F reaches a frequency of >75% in three patients but is rare or nonexistent in influenza globally (Figure 4D), suggesting that this mutation may have within-host benefits that are not reflected in global evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutation L427F may have within-host benefits that are not reflected in global evolution.
source: Mutation L427F reaches a frequency of >75% in three patients but is rare or nonexistent in influenza globally (Figure 4D), suggesting that this mutation may have within-host benefits that are not reflected in global evolution.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion in the Results section based on the observation of high within-host frequency but low global frequency.

claim: The four HA sites that displayed parallel within-host and global evolution (138, 193, 223, and 225) also gave rise to mutations in laboratory-passaged influenza isolated longitudinally from an immunocompromised child.
source: Notably, the four HA sites that displayed parallel within-host and global evolution in our study (138, 193, 223, and 225) also gave rise to mutations in another study that used Sanger sequencing to analyze laboratory-passaged influenza isolated longitudinally from an immunocompromised child (Baz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Baz et al., 2006.

claim: Antigenic drift of influenza within an immunocompromised patient resembled global antigenic change.
source: Another previous study used hemagglutination inhibition assays to show that antigenic drift of influenza within an immunocompromised patient resembled global antigenic change (McMinn et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to McMinn et al., 1999.

claim: In HIV, similar mutations can arise within hosts that share an HLA type, but tend to revert upon transmission to recipients with different HLA types.
source: The parallel evolution that we observe in influenza at the within-host and global scales contrasts with HIV, where similar mutations can arise within hosts that share an HLA type, but tend to revert upon transmission to recipients with different HLA types (Leslie et al., 2004; Herbeck et al., 2006; Lemey et al., 2006; Zanini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to multiple HIV studies.

claim: Immune epitopes in influenza are broadly similar among individuals, with some exceptions.
source: Part of the difference may be that immune epitopes in influenza are broadly similar among individuals, with some exceptions (Li et al., 2013; Linderman et al., 2014), whereas the targets of anti-HIV immunity vary more widely due to patient-specific factors like HLA type.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Li et al., 2013 and Linderman et al., 2014.

claim: The targets of anti-HIV immunity vary more widely than influenza due to patient-specific factors like HLA type.
source: Part of the difference may be that immune epitopes in influenza are broadly similar among individuals, with some exceptions (Li et al., 2013; Linderman et al., 2014), whereas the targets of anti-HIV immunity vary more widely due to patient-specific factors like HLA type.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison to influenza.

claim: Prior studies sampling from acute infections of immunocompetent hosts found limited within-host variation in influenza.
source: The parallelism and extensive evolution that we observe in long-term influenza infections contrasts with the limited within-host variation found in prior studies, which sample from acute infections of immunocompetent hosts (Murcia et al., 2010; Hoelzer et al., 2010; Dinis et al., 2016; Debbink et al., 2017; Sobel Leonard et al., 2016; Poon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: A recent study deep-sequenced HA from several hundred patients but only found a small number of antigenic variants, mostly at low frequencies.
source: For instance, one recent study deep-sequenced HA from several hundred patients but only found a small number of antigenic variants, and mostly at low frequencies (Dinis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Dinis et al., 2016.

claim: Influenza may experience many of the same selective pressures within acute infections as it does globally, even if short infection durations make it difficult for selected mutations to reach detectable frequencies.
source: But our study suggests that influenza may experience many of the same selective pressures within acute infections as it does globally, even if the short durations of these infections make it difficult for selected mutations to reach frequencies that are detectable with current methods.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Within-host viral diversity may act as a noisy early measurement of global viral evolution.
source: We suggest that within-host viral diversity may act as a noisy early measurement of global viral evolution, shaped by some of the same immunological and evolutionary constraints.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion in the Discussion section based on the study's findings.

claim: Samples were prospectively collected during a surveillance study for respiratory viruses performed in allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients undergoing transplantation between December 2005 and February 2010 at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center.
source: Samples were prospectively collected during a surveillance study for respiratory viruses performed in allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HCT) recipients undergoing transplantation between December 2005 and February 2010 at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (Campbell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citation to Campbell et al., 2015.

claim: Weekly nasal wash samples were obtained at least once before and weekly after HCT up to 100 days.
source: Following written informed consent, weekly nasal wash samples (or nasopharyngeal swabs if nasal wash samples were precluded clinically) and oropharyngeal swab specimens were obtained at least once before and weekly after HCT up to 100 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing sample collection.

claim: Samples were considered positive if the assay's cycle threshold was less than 40, for a limit of detection of approximately 2000 viral copies/mL.
source: Samples were considered positive if the assay's cycle threshold was less than 40, for a limit of detection of approximately 2000 viral copies/mL.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the detection threshold.

claim: All samples sequenced in this study tested positive for influenza A.
source: All samples sequenced in this study tested positive for influenza A.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Patient W was a female in the 25-44 age group who developed upper respiratory symptoms in early 2007, 30 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for Hodgkin's disease.
source: A female in the 25–44 age group developed upper respiratory symptoms in early 2007, 30 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for Hodgkin's disease and 18 days following engraftment.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient W.

claim: Patient W's nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A for 80 days until the patient died of pulmonary failure.
source: Patient nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A for the next 80 days until the patient died of pulmonary failure, with diffuse alveolar damage found on autopsy.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient W's clinical course.

claim: Patient W was co-infected with coronavirus for the duration of the influenza infection.
source: The patient was co-infected with coronavirus for the duration of the influenza infection and also tested positive for human metapneumovirus for the last 26 days of her life.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient W.

claim: Patient X was a male in the 65+ age group who developed upper respiratory symptoms in early 2006, 45 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for Hodgkin's disease.
source: A male in the 65+ age group developed upper respiratory symptoms in early 2006, 45 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for Hodgkin's disease.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient X.

claim: Patient X's nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A for 72 days, after which the patient chose to discontinue study participation.
source: Patient nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A for the next 72 days, after which the patient chose to discontinue study participation.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient X.

claim: Patient Y was a male in the 45-64 age group who developed upper respiratory symptoms in spring 2006, 62 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for acute myeloid leukemia.
source: A male in the 45–64 age group developed upper respiratory symptoms in spring 2006, 62 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and 52 days after engraftment.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient Y.

claim: Patient Y's nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A for 77 days, after which the patient began testing negative.
source: Patient nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A for the next 77 days, after which the patient began testing negative.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient Y.

claim: Patient Z was a male in the 65+ age group who developed upper respiratory symptoms in early 2007, 197 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for AML.
source: A male in the 65+ age group developed upper respiratory symptoms in early 2007, 197 days after receiving a non-myeloablative HCT for AML and 175 days after engraftment.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient Z.

claim: Patient Z's nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A over 69 days, after which monitoring ceased due to severe illness, and the patient died 15 days after the last influenza-positive sample from relapsed AML.
source: Nasal wash samples repeatedly tested positive for influenza A over the next 69 days, after which monitoring ceased due to severe illness, and the patient died 15 days after the last influenza-positive sample from relapsed AML.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing Patient Z.

claim: Eight low-quality samples were excluded from downstream analyses due to low sequencing coverage or variant frequencies differing greatly between replicates.
source: We excluded from downstream analyses eight low-quality samples for which sequencing coverage was low or variant frequencies differed greatly between replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sequencing libraries were prepared in duplicate for each sample, beginning from separate reverse-transcription reactions.
source: To limit the impact of library preparation and sequencing errors on estimates of variant frequency (McCrone and Lauring, 2016), we prepared sequencing libraries in duplicate for each sample, beginning from separate reverse-transcription reactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to McCrone and Lauring, 2016.

claim: The full viral genome was sequenced to high coverage directly from patient nasal wash samples using influenza-specific reverse transcription and PCR.
source: We sequenced the full viral genome to high coverage directly from patient nasal wash samples by using influenza-specific reverse transcription and PCR (Hoffmann et al., 2001) to enrich for viral genetic material (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Hoffmann et al., 2001.

claim: Many nonsynonymous mutations occur at sites that affect the antigenicity of HA.
source: Many nonsynonymous mutations occur at sites that affect the antigenicity of HA (Koel et al., 2013) and the antiviral sensitivity of NA (Baz et al., 2006; van der Vries et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Koel et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Many nonsynonymous mutations occur at sites that affect the antiviral sensitivity of NA.
source: Many nonsynonymous mutations occur at sites that affect the antigenicity of HA (Koel et al., 2013) and the antiviral sensitivity of NA (Baz et al., 2006; van der Vries et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Baz et al., 2006 and van der Vries et al., 2013.

claim: Influenza rapidly acquires de novo mutations as it replicates within infected hosts.
source: Viruses rapidly acquire de novo mutations as they replicate within infected hosts (Andino and Domingo, 2015), but only a small fraction of these variants transmit between hosts and eventually fix on a global scale.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation to Andino and Domingo, 2015.

claim: Only a small fraction of within-host viral variants transmit between hosts and eventually fix on a global scale.
source: Viruses rapidly acquire de novo mutations as they replicate within infected hosts (Andino and Domingo, 2015), but only a small fraction of these variants transmit between hosts and eventually fix on a global scale.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction.

claim: Transmission bottlenecks shape viral genetic diversity at larger scales of space and time.
source: At larger scales of space and time, transmission bottlenecks (Varble et al., 2014; Poon et al., 2016) and host heterogeneity also shape viral genetic diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to Varble et al., 2014 and Poon et al., 2016.

claim: Host heterogeneity shapes viral genetic diversity at larger scales of space and time.
source: At larger scales of space and time, transmission bottlenecks (Varble et al., 2014; Poon et al., 2016) and host heterogeneity also shape viral genetic diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction.

claim: Recent deep-sequencing studies of human clinical samples suggest that influenza accumulates relatively limited genetic diversity within hosts during most acute infections.
source: Recent deep-sequencing studies of human clinical samples suggest that influenza accumulates relatively limited genetic diversity within hosts during most acute infections (Dinis et al., 2016; Poon et al., 2016; Sobel Leonard et al., 2016; Debbink et al., 2017), in line with earlier studies in dogs and horses (Murcia et al., 2010; Hoelzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Earlier studies in dogs and horses found that influenza accumulates limited genetic diversity within hosts.
source: Recent deep-sequencing studies of human clinical samples suggest that influenza accumulates relatively limited genetic diversity within hosts during most acute infections (Dinis et al., 2016; Poon et al., 2016; Sobel Leonard et al., 2016; Debbink et al., 2017), in line with earlier studies in dogs and horses (Murcia et al., 2010; Hoelzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to Murcia et al., 2010 and Hoelzer et al., 2010.

claim: Some within-host mutations may confer novel antigenic properties.
source: Some within-host mutations may confer novel antigenic properties (Dinis et al., 2016), but most lack clear functional interpretation.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation to Dinis et al., 2016.

claim: Most within-host mutations lack clear functional interpretation.
source: Some within-host mutations may confer novel antigenic properties (Dinis et al., 2016), but most lack clear functional interpretation.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction.

claim: Influenza infections usually last less than a week.
source: Influenza infections usually last less than a week and provide limited opportunity for longitudinal study.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction.

claim: Among some immunocompromised patients, influenza infections can last weeks or months.
source: But among some immunocompromised patients, infections can last weeks or months (Nichols et al., 2004; Memoli et al., 2014), making it possible to examine longer-term within-host evolutionary dynamics (Rocha et al., 1991; McMinn et al., 1999; Rogers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to Nichols et al., 2004 and Memoli et al., 2014.

claim: Long-term influenza infections in immunocompromised patients make it possible to examine longer-term within-host evolutionary dynamics.
source: But among some immunocompromised patients, infections can last weeks or months (Nichols et al., 2004; Memoli et al., 2014), making it possible to examine longer-term within-host evolutionary dynamics (Rocha et al., 1991; McMinn et al., 1999; Rogers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to studies examining within-host dynamics.

claim: Influenza evolution within infected humans recapitulates many evolutionary dynamics observed at the global scale.
source: Here, we demonstrate that influenza evolution within infected humans recapitulates many evolutionary dynamics observed at the global scale.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Parallel evolution occurs across three scales: within individual patients, in different patients in the study, and in the global influenza population.
source: We find parallel evolution across three scales: within individual patients, in different patients in our study, and in the global influenza population.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: In hemagglutinin, a small set of mutations arises independently in multiple patients.
source: In hemagglutinin, a small set of mutations arises independently in multiple patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: The same mutations emerge repeatedly within single patients and compete with one another, providing a clinical example of clonal interference.
source: These same mutations emerge repeatedly within single patients and compete with one another, providing a vivid clinical example of clonal interference.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Many recurrent within-host mutations reach a high global frequency in the decade following the patient infections.
source: Many of these recurrent within-host mutations also reach a high global frequency in the decade following the patient infections.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: The study demonstrates surprising concordance in evolutionary dynamics across multiple spatiotemporal scales.
source: Our results demonstrate surprising concordance in evolutionary dynamics across multiple spatiotemporal scales.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as the main conclusion.

claim: The unpredictability of clonal competition determines which mutations eventually fix.
source: Although many of these beneficial mutations are selected in parallel in multiple patients, the unpredictability of clonal competition determines which mutations eventually fix.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the haplotype analysis.

claim: In large, clonally evolving influenza populations within hosts, a small set of beneficial mutations repeatedly arise and compete against one another in various combinations.
source: Our analysis shows that in large, clonally evolving influenza populations within hosts, a small set of beneficial mutations repeatedly arise and compete against one another in various combinations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the haplotype analysis.

claim: Parallelism in HA evolution may emerge from the confluence of several evolutionary conditions: concordant selection across environments, a constrained evolutionary landscape, and sufficiently large population sizes, high mutation rates, and time.
source: We suggest that parallelism in HA evolution may emerge from the confluence of several evolutionary conditions (Lässig et al., 2017). First, if selection acts concordantly across environments, it will favor a common set of beneficial mutations. Second, in a constrained evolutionary landscape, this set of beneficial mutations will be relatively small. Finally, given sufficiently large population sizes, high mutation rates, and time, these beneficial mutations will emerge and be selected to detectable frequencies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed explanation with citation to Lässig et al., 2017.

claim: Influenza may experience many of the same selective pressures within acute infections as it does globally.
source: But our study suggests that influenza may experience many of the same selective pressures within acute infections as it does globally, even if the short durations of these infections make it difficult for selected mutations to reach frequencies that are detectable with current methods.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Detailed characterization of within-host variation will be increasingly valuable for understanding how molecular, immunological, and epidemiological forces interact to shape viral evolution.
source: As high-throughput sequencing continues to improve, detailed characterization of within-host variation will be increasingly valuable for understanding how molecular, immunological, and epidemiological forces interact to shape viral evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a forward-looking statement.
